At a time when the average movie-goer is getting increasingly skeptical of 'hacking scenes' that showcase multi-dimensional Rubik's cubes interlinked in cyberspace, Hacknet does a pretty good job of capturing that disillusionment with a game that's closer to reality.

This game could be used to simulate hacking in movies, especially since you can create custom extensions/mods with their own back stories.

Pro's

+ Not much of a fancy GUI or Hollywood-style effects. It's possible to disable the GUI and go terminal-only.
+ Real unix commands to interact with the file system.

Con's

- Might feel lacklustre if you have used Linux before and/or already know some security jargon.

This game is pretty dope.

Gameplay-wise, the actual inputs you'll perform are mainly terminal based. Most of the time you'll be typing commands as rapidly as you can. Actual inputs can be tricky if you need to operate quickly, but the majority of what you'll be doing is essentially puzzle solving. A typical mission in the game requires you to gain access to a given entry point which will contain links or clues that you can follow to the next point, which may contain further clues, etc. That's an incredibly basic description of the game: Actual missions are immersive enough and the actual hints/puzzles/solutions are varied enough that the game is able to stay fresh well through the main campaign and DLC.

The story is pretty cool. (Won't go into spoilers here, what I tell you is what you learn literally within minutes of starting the game.) A notorious hacker who goes by Bit has passed away, and has left you his custom-made hacking software in his wake, along with the request to use it to figure out what killed him and why. You quickly integrate with a local hacker group and start climbing the ranks to gain influence and leads. Along the way you'll acquire (either from your hacker group or by stealing it from a target computer) new tools or methods that allow you to break into more secure devices. Since the game is all text based, you'll only get to know characters via what they've written to you, and it can be tricky to build strong characters that way if the player is impatient. I feel that sticking through and reading the text will greatly benefit your enjoyment of the story of the game as well as of the game overall.

The aesthetic of the game is a big part of it. The entire game is played as though it's not a game. It's as if you have a virtual machine running another OS on your computer. The perspective is never pulled into real life, and you'll never see your character because as far as the game is concerned, YOU in real life are your character. This is an excellent way to build immersion, and you'll find yourself quickly sucked in to the game. The visuals are simplistic but robust and well designed (and even customizable, eventually), and the soundtrack will keep you cool while trying to break into complex systems and get you pumped when it's time to move fast. Just playing the game and becoming immersed is a bit of an experience that can be hard to find elsewhere.

As an aside, I would reccomend the DLC if you enjoy the main game. It tells a story that's basically completely separate from the main game: Essentially it may as well be a sequel. It introduces new systems that compliment the puzzle elements like I mentioned above. The game also features workshop support which contains even more community made campaigns (some as long as the DLC), but many of them require content from the DLC to function.

Tl;dr: Fun game, you'll get immersed if you let yourself and it's a serious blast. Gameplay is essentially puzzle based but at times requires you to be fast too.

The game is fun.  It has both a GUI and commandline for whichever you are most comfortable with.  At a couple parts, the more intrepid players will find things beyond their means or things they are supposed to discover a little later after explanation that they do not really know what to do with, but that's fine.  I like games that allow you to do that.  There are a lot of funny/entertaining logs to read and it's apparent that there is a lot of thought that went into the story behind it.

Gameplay-wise, though, it wasn't as much as it could be.  A couple hours into it and I realize I'm basically just playing Linux with some commands missing.  That isn't to say I'm not entertained so far, definitely worth it to buy, but if you're familiar with Linux and know your way around the terminal, it won't be anything new and the lack of commands can be a little jarring once you get in your groove.

Another thing, it's definitely a GPU hog.  My GPU was going nuts, especially if I alt-tabbed.  Was getting up to 90c with fans going max.

Overall, though, good game, is fun.  Plan on finishing it when I get some more time to play.

It's funny how a game with virtually no graphics and a gameplay consisting of posting commands to command prompt has a deeper immersion than most of other games.
This game is quite creative, and the only thing I played which is similar to this is Uplink, though Hacknet has a way better UI, and, also, a story (!) 
Surprisingly I enjoyed this game greatly, especially a moment, where game virtually breaks the 4th wall, crashing and opening a command prompt on your actual Desktop, refusing to launch, unless you delete a 'virus' from your system.
I know, game looks a bit gimmicky and actual hacking is nowhere near like that, but it's still fun and supposed to be taken lightly as a piece of fiction.
Also, did I mention music? Because music _really_ makes this game for me. At some point it plays chilled Resonance by Home, and then it switches to teethgrinding tracks from Carpenter Brut, creating a sense of urgency and dread.
If I were to describe this game in one word, I'd say COZY. Because, that's how I felt, looking at outrun-styled background, listening to Resonance and 'hacking' some plebs.
I'm really glad this game 'clicked' for me, and I enjoyed it way more, that I expected to.
So, if you're into (pop)cyberpunk, 80-s, outrun and synth-music, this game might be just the right game for you.
p.s get this game with Labyrinths add-on, it adds a great deal of gameplay, fantastic music and irc "chat"

A really great game!

Important to note that the game is story-driven. There's no money, economy or upgradable equipment.
I personally expected something more like Uplink.

There's also the "issue" of realism, which is obviously quite low. Makes the game really easy to get into, but I'd be surprised if some people wouldn't have a problem with this.

[h1]Sounds[/h1]
Awesome, ever-changing music. No extremes in it and fitting for the game.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The aesthetics are really good looking. There isn't much going on in that regard of course, but what you see looks good.
I'd say that the server map gets a bit too crowded towards the end, but you're usually well-guided and there's almost no need to backtrack, so it's not that big of a deal.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The commands you need to use are introduced one by one, giving you time to get used to.
They're aptly named and the autocomplete function helps a lot.
There's an easy to use Note system (hence the no need for backtracking).

Sometimes you have to work fast, and that means you're in danger, which raises 2 small issues:
1. the need to type fast or at least at decent speed which I imagine can be limiting for some players.
2. "delete line" key or combination.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The main story itself is decent. It's not really something that makes you think or makes you emotionally invested.
The logs are interesting enough though, especially for a game where you have to read all the time.
I really liked some of the IRC logs as well, nice touch.
Most importantly the ending is not empty at all.


All things considered there are no serious problems with the game, and lots of great things about it!

Surprisingly fun, despite the lack of whiz-bang graphics that we've grown accustomed to. 
The intensity builds up slowly and missions get incrementally harder. 
The tasks are somewhat repetitive although having a programmable keyboard helps overcome the mundaneity of having to type the same commands over and over again. analyze analyze analyze analyze - in this day and age, should there not be a command that says Analyze times five or something? Thankfully, there was also a sufficient dose of humor sprinkled throughout the game to keep me interested when things got a bit tired.
Overall, the storyline is compelling enough although the end seemed kind of rushed. I wanted more from it in terms of the payback, which did not seem commensurate with the absolute evil that was done. But that could be just me.

NB. the game was interesting enough to entice me to pick up the sequel, so kudos to the developers.
